content: A developing country is characterized by a relatively low standard of living, an underdeveloped industrial base, and moderate to low scores on the Human Development Index (HDI) and per capita income. However, such countries are typically in a phase of economic development. While the term developing country is often used to describe nations that are neither fully developed nor failed states, this classification is not universally accurate. Some developing countries exhibit levels of development that surpass those of certain developed nations. Nations with economies that are more advanced than other developing countries but have not yet fully demonstrated the characteristics of a developed country are referred to as newly industrialized countries (NICs). Other developing nations that have achieved sustained economic growth over time and show strong economic potential are classified as emerging markets. Examples of Big Emerging Market (BEM) economies include Argentina, Brazil, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Poland, Russia, South Africa, South Korea, and Turkey. The application of the term developing country to any nation that is not developed is considered inappropriate in some cases, as certain poor countries have experienced prolonged periods of economic decline. These nations are categorized as either least developed countries (LDCs) or failed states. Development, in its essence, involves the establishment of modern infrastructure—both physical and institutional—and a shift away from low-value-added sectors such as agriculture and natural resource extraction. In contrast, developed countries typically have economic systems based on continuous, self-sustaining growth in the tertiary and quaternary sectors, along with high standards of living. The level of development in a country is measured using statistical indices such as income per capita (GDP), life expectancy, and literacy rates. The United Nations has developed the Human Development Index (HDI), a composite indicator that combines these statistics to assess the level of human development in countries where data is available. Developing countries, in general, are those that have not achieved significant industrialization relative to their populations and have a low standard of living. There is a strong correlation between low income and high population growth in these nations. The terminology used to describe developing countries often reflects the intent and perspective of those employing these terms. Other terms sometimes used include less developed countries (LDCs), least economically developed countries (LEDCs), underdeveloped nations, Third World nations, and non-industrialized nations. Conversely, the opposite end of the spectrum is referred to as developed countries, most economically developed countries (MEDCs), First World nations, or industrialized nations. To address the euphemistic nature of the term developing, international organizations have begun using the term less economically developed countries (LEDCs) to describe the poorest nations that cannot reasonably be considered as developing. LEDCs represent the poorest subset of LDCs. This distinction also helps to counter the misconception that the standard of living is uniform across the entire developing world. The concept of a developing nation is present in various theoretical frameworks, including decolonization theories, liberation theology, Marxism, anti-imperialism, and political economy. Critics argue that the term developing can sometimes be a misnomer. In the case of countries that were devastated by European colonialism, the term re-developing may be more accurate, as many of these nations had successful economic systems prior to colonization. However, due to ethnocentrism, Western analysts often dismiss these pre-colonial systems as invalid and fail to recognize them as developed. The underlying assumption is that to develop is synonymous with to develop in a Western manner. Emerging and developing economies, as identified by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in its World Economic Outlook Report, include a wide range of nations. Newly industrialized countries (NICs) are those with economies that are more advanced than other developing nations but have not yet reached the full characteristics of developed countries. Examples of NICs include Brazil, China, India, Malaysia, Mexico, the Philippines, South Africa, Thailand, and Turkey. Additionally, Big Emerging Market (BEM) economies include nations such as Argentina, Brazil, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Mexico, Poland, Russia, South Africa, South Korea, and Turkey. Globally, approximately 76% of countries fall under the category of developing or emerging economies. However, some nations, such as Afghanistan, Haiti, Somalia, Myanmar, Iraq, and North Korea, are often classified as failed states due to prolonged instability and low resource availability.
